metadata.title: BloomAPR: A Bloom's Taxonomy-based Framework for Assessing the Capabilities of LLM-Powered APR Solutions

abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have accelerated the development of AI-driven automated program repair (APR) solutions. However, these solutions are typically evaluated using static benchmarks such as Defects4J and SWE-bench, which suffer from two key limitations: (1) the risk of data contamination, potentially inflating evaluation results due to overlap with LLM training data, and (2) limited ability to assess the APR capabilities in dynamic and diverse contexts. In this paper, we introduced BloomAPR, a novel dynamic evaluation framework grounded in Bloom's Taxonomy. Our framework offers a structured approach to assess the cognitive capabilities of LLM-powered APR solutions across progressively complex reasoning levels. Using Defects4J as a case study, we evaluated two state-of-the-art LLM-powered APR solutions, ChatRepair and CigaR, under three different LLMs: GPT-3.5-Turbo, Llama-3.1, and StarCoder-2. Our findings show that while these solutions exhibit basic reasoning skills and effectively memorize bug-fixing patterns (fixing up to 81.57% of bugs at the Remember layer), their performance increases with synthetically generated bugs (up to 60.66% increase at the Understand layer). However, they perform worse on minor syntactic changes (fixing up to 43.32% at the Apply layer), and they struggle to repair similar bugs when injected into real-world projects (solving only 13.46% to 41.34% bugs at the Analyze layer). These results underscore the urgent need for evolving benchmarks and provide a foundation for more trustworthy evaluation of LLM-powered software engineering solutions.

poised to transform our society significantly [18, 56]. Take software engineering (SE), for example. LLMs have shown
great promise and are expected to revolutionize the entire software engineering lifecycle [26, 45, 65]. Companies and
SE professionals have already begun adopting LLM-powered tools to boost their productivity [17, 62] and enhance
software quality [22, 63, 78]. The research progress (e.g., [2, 37, 75, 79]) in this area is primarily demonstrated on publicly
available benchmarks (e.g., Defects4J [35], HumanEval [12] and SWE-Bench [34]).
Although the use of these benchmarks facilitates cross-comparison and replication, the reported results can suffer
from data contamination due to the overlap between the training and the evaluation datasets [57, 83]. Consequently,
the benchmark results may not accurately reflect true model capabilities and reveal their deficiencies [52, 72]. However,
faithfully evaluating the capabilities of LLM-powered SE solutions presents the following challenges:
• The LLM side: There are over 270 existing SE benchmarks [9], with new ones continuously curated or updated
based on real-world datasets [20, 44]. Although data decontamination procedures can be applied during LLM training
to deliberately search for and remove benchmark datasets from the training corpus [23, 47], it remains challenging to
comprehensively identify and exclude all benchmark data and their associated tasks from the pre-training datasets to
ensure trustworthiness.
• The benchmark side: Existing benchmarks are used not only for evaluation and cross-comparison [55] but also for
performance tuning and debugging during research and tool development [25, 74, 75]. This dual use makes it difficult
to keep benchmarks open and reusable for the community while simultaneously avoiding contamination, which is
crucial for faithful evaluation. Recently, dynamic benchmarking techniques have been proposed to continuously
curate fresh data [4, 20, 30, 44, 48] to minimize the overlap between the training and the evaluation datasets. However,
newly curated datasets may not closely resemble the same characteristics (e.g., difficulty levels and skill sets) as the
original benchmarks, making it difficult to accurately track the progression of a model’s capabilities [32].
• The LLM-powered solution side: Studies show that LLM-powered SE solutions can be brittle, even in response
to small code perturbations [66, 71, 83]. Unfortunately, many evaluations assess LLM-powered solutions solely on
the benchmarks as they are, often overlooking robustness, except [55], which employs basic mutation techniques
(e.g., operator and literal mutations). Since such synthetic mutations may not accurately capture the complexity of
real-world bugs [15, 36], there is a need for novel evaluation methodologies that can more comprehensively and
realistically assess the capabilities of a given solution.

BloomAPR: A Bloom’s Taxonomy-based Framework for Assessing the Capabilities of LLM-Powered APR Solutions 3
To address the above three challenges, we argue that rather than focusing solely on the difficult task of eliminating
overlap between the benchmark and the LLM’s training datasets, the research community should prioritize the
development of innovative evaluation methodologies that can robustly assess LLM-powered SE solutions across
diverse usage contexts. Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel evaluation framework that systematically assesses
the capabilities of LLM-powered solutions by incorporating Bloom’s Taxonomy [5, 6]. As shown in Figure 1, Bloom’s
Taxonomy classifies cognitive abilities into six layers of increasing complexity, ranging from lower-order thinking skills
that require basic cognitive processing (Remember, Understand, Apply) to higher-order thinking skills that require
more advanced and deeper cognitive processing (Analyze, Evaluate, Create). Originally designed for educational
settings, it has been widely adopted to structure learning objectives and design assessments. Integrating Bloom’s
Taxonomy into the evaluation framework enables fine-grained identification of specific competencies demonstrated by a
solution and highlights areas for improvement [28, 83]. Since our framework builds upon existing static benchmarks, the
evaluation results are easily trackable and comparable, thereby ensuring consistency. To demonstrate the feasibility and
effectiveness of our framework, we developed a research prototype, BloomAPR, based on the well-known Defects4J
benchmark and evaluated it on two state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLM-powered Automated Program Repair (APR) solutions:
ChatRepair [75] and CigaR [25]. For each bug in the original benchmark, our framework generates multiple variations
and synthesizes new versions to ensure robust evaluation. Our evaluation results show that both solutions are primarily
limited to basic recall (solving 53.92% to 82.71% of issues at the Remember layer). They reach a higher plausible patch
rate when dealing with the synthetic code structure (88.94% to 98.61% for Fix_+ and Fix_A at the Understand layer),
and then their performance drops at the Apply layer under LLM-generated rephrasing-based renaming and hash-based
renaming settings (21.66% to 50.69%), showing difficulty in handling semantic variations. They also have difficulty
analyzing in similar but slightly different real-world contexts and applying the learned skills (13.46% to 41.34% for
Fix_+ and Fix_A at the Analyze layer). The discrepancy between the Analyze layer and the lower layers highlights
their weakness in handling large code contexts. The contributions of this paper are:
• This paper introduces BloomAPR, the first systematic framework that transforms an existing static APR benchmark
into a structured, dynamic evaluation environment grounded in Bloom’s Taxonomy. Unlike existing benchmarking
approaches, BloomAPR organizes evaluation tasks into layers that diagnose different cognitive capabilities of LLM-
powered APR agents. Our framework not only mitigates data-contamination and robustness issues common to static
benchmarks, but also addresses consistency limitations and faithfulness concerns in current dynamic benchmarks.
To our knowledge, this is the first work to transform existing static benchmarks into structured dynamic evaluations
grounded in Bloom’s Taxonomy.
• While we reuse existing perturbation and memorization checks where applicable (e.g., at the Remember and Apply
layers), we introduce new evaluation techniques—such as controlled bug injections and synthetic bug generation
across diverse project contexts at the Understand and Analyze layers. This layered structure enables not only raw
accuracy reporting but also cross-layer insights into why APR agents succeed or fail.
• Prior empirical studies on the impact of data contamination in software engineering tasks (e.g., [57, 83]) have
focused on direct LLM prompting. In contrast, BloomAPR evaluates APR agents that employ agentic workflows
(reflection, test-time sampling, iterative debugging), which iteratively refine bug fixes using the compiler, testing
results, and contextual cues (e.g., code snippets or test cases). Our experiments reveal that these workflows do not
automatically mitigate contamination effects, highlighting new research needs in reasoning and generalization for

2
Background and Related Work
In this section, we discuss the background and existing research related to our work.
2.1
Automated Program Repair (APR)
APR solutions automatically identify and fix software bugs without human intervention. Traditional APR solutions often
rely on generate-and-validate approaches, where candidate patches are generated and tested against a suite of test cases
to ensure correctness [31, 46, 69, 82]. Learning-based APR techniques utilize various information sources (e.g., historical
bug-fix data) to predict potential patches, thereby improving the efficiency and accuracy of repairs [14, 33, 80, 81].
Large Language Model (LLM)-based APR solutions utilize LLMs’ advanced capabilities to identify and fix bugs in
software code automatically. Unlike traditional generate-and-validate approaches, LLM-powered APR solutions leverage
the extensive pre-trained knowledge of LLMs to generate potential patches directly from the context of the entire
program [3, 7, 43, 77]. Consistent with prior works [25, 73–75], we evaluated the effectiveness of APR agents using
well-known metrics like Exact Match (EM), SYntactic Equivalence (SYE), and Plausible Patches (PP).
2.2
Data Contamination
Data contamination occurs when information from the test set is unintentionally included in the training set, leading
to inflated performance metrics and compromised model evaluation. In the context of LLMs, data contamination can
significantly affect the evaluation fairness, making it difficult to assess the model’s true capabilities accurately. Prior
studies [32, 36, 58, 60] have witnessed such influence and proposed various ways to mitigate the problem. To avoid data
contamination, Jiang et. al. constructed HumanEval-Java [32] by manually converting HumanEval Python programs to
Java and injecting bugs into the correct Java programs. Meanwhile, RepairBench [60], which includes GitBug-Java [61],
featuring recent bugs from 2023, beyond the training cut-off date of most LLMs—and Defects4J, is proposed as a
framework for the standardized evaluation of frontier APR solutions. However, due to their static nature, i.e., having a
fixed set of evaluation tasks, the problems will persist as models evolve and re-train over time [16, 59, 76].

To assess the impact of data contamination and the ability of APRs to generalize, we not only reused some existing
approaches but also introduced novel evaluation techniques. In particular, we reused existing membership inference
techniques [10, 84] at the Remember layer to examine the overlap of the training dataset and the target benchmark.
However, this result alone does not reveal the impact of memorization on APR effectiveness. Therefore, we re-ran
and re-evaluated APR agents on the original benchmark and evaluated the results to assess their impact. The name
perturbation technique at the Apply layer is similar to [83]. However, as we want to assess the effectiveness of APR
under semantic variations, we evaluated the impact of two perturbation techniques: rephrasing-based renaming and
hash-based renaming. The controlled bug injections and synthetic bug generation across diverse project contexts at the
Understand and Analyze layers are novel and are intended to assess the APR performance under logical and context
variations, respectively.
2.3
Dynamic Benchmarking
Dynamic benchmarking has emerged as a promising approach for evaluating LLMs, mitigating the limitations of
static benchmarks that are prone to data contamination and fail to keep pace with rapidly advancing generation
capabilities [11, 39, 67]. Key features of dynamic benchmarking include: (1) adaptive evaluation, tailoring more complex
tasks as models advance over time [86, 88]; (2) mitigation of data contamination by generating novel, out-of-distribution
scenarios [13, 27]; and (3) fine-grained capability assessment that dissects specific cognitive abilities such as reasoning
and problem-solving [27, 89]. For instance, DyVal [88] utilizes directed acyclic graphs (DAG) to create structured
reasoning tasks with controllable complexity, while DyVal2 employs meta-probing agents inspired by psychometric
theories to transform existing problems into new challenges targeting specific cognitive skills. Similarly, DARG [86]
constructs and perturbs reasoning graphs to generate diverse test samples, enabling a more comprehensive evaluation
of LLMs’ generalization and robustness.
While dynamic benchmarking has gained traction in evaluating LLMs, it remains underexplored in APR tasks. Recent
studies have introduced dynamic benchmarking frameworks in ASE that apply semantic-preserving mutations to code
benchmarks, creating syntactically new yet semantically identical programs [13, 24, 54]. These approaches aim to
mitigate data contamination and better assess the robustness of code understanding and reasoning models. However,
the integration of such dynamic benchmarking methodologies for the APR task remains unexplored. To address these
challenges, we propose the BloomAPR framework, which incorporates dynamic benchmarking to robustly and reliably
evaluate LLMs for the APR task by adapting to their evolving capabilities at various cognitive layers and mitigating
data contamination.
3
Our Evaluation Framework
In this section, we describe our evaluation framework, BloomAPR, which systemically assesses the capabilities of LLM-
powered APR solutions. As illustrated in Figure 1, our framework is conceptually divided into six layers, corresponding
to the Bloom’s Taxonomy: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create.
Our framework leverages high-quality data from publicly available static bug-fixing benchmarks to facilitate cross-
comparison and performance tuning. Depending on the objectives of each layer, variations of each bug instance from
the adopted benchmarks are generated using techniques such as program transformation, data synthesis, and bug
injection. Bloom’s taxonomy is hierarchical, meaning each layer builds on and assumes the competencies of those
below it. To demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of BloomAPR, we developed our research prototype based on
version 2.1.0 of the Defects4J benchmark. In our design, the Remember layer evaluates whether SUEs can retrieve or

recognize known fixes or patterns from a bug-fixing benchmark. For each bug instance in the original Defects4J, the
subsequent layers deliberately increase difficulty and novelty in a controlled manner:
• Logical variations: the Understand layer tests whether SUEs can grasp the underlying bug logic through simple
synthetically LLM-generated bug instances that preserve bug semantics while avoiding lexical overlap.
• Lexical variations: the Analyze layer probes brittleness by introducing surface-level synthetic variations via
behavior-preserving transformations (e.g., variable or function renaming).
• Context variations: the Apply layer further increases complexity by placing bugs into diverse real-world project
contexts with external dependencies.
In this initial prototype, we did not address the top two advanced reasoning layers: Evaluate and Create. The
Evaluate layer focuses on patch assessment and selection, which is often treated as a related but distinct research
problem (e.g., [40, 41, 87]). The Create layer targets the generation of new bug types and fixes, a capability that current
APR tools cannot yet achieve. The remainder of this section explains each layer in detail. To aid explanation, we use a
running example to illustrate how an existing bug instance from Defects4J, is transformed across different layers.
3.1
Remember
Objective: The goal of the evaluation at the Remember layer is to check whether the LLM-powered APR solutions under
evaluation (SUEs) can recall or recognize facts about the target bug-fixing benchmark (Defects4J).
Approach: As existing studies show that LLMs may memorize bug benchmarks [57, 83], it is very likely that many
existing bug benchmarks have already been included as part of the training datasets. Hence, at the Remember layer of
BloomAPR, we only included 217 bug instances (single-function-level bugs), which are added only from version 2.1.0 of
the Defects4J, and intentionally removed bugs from the previous version (v1.0.0). The APR solution under evaluation
(SUE) will be executed against these 217 bug instances to check whether these solutions can retrieve known bug fixes
or recognize bug-fixing patterns as a result of their training process.
Evaluation Schemes: These three metrics will be tracked:
• % bugs with plausible patches (PP): PPs refer to bug fixes that pass all the given tests. % of bugs with PP is an optimistic
measure, as some of the plausible patches may fail on additional test cases that are not included. Hence, it provides
an upper bound in terms of how well the evaluated solutions can recognize known bug-fixing patterns.
• % bugs with exact matches (EM) patches: EMs refer to bug fixes that exactly match the provided oracle. While there
may be multiple valid ways to fix a bug, a high percentage of EMs is a strong indicator of the SUEs’ effectiveness.
For each PP and its corresponding oracle code snippets, we removed comments and whitespace, then compared the
resulting string sequences directly. If they were equal, the patch was classified as an EM.
• % bugs with SYntactic Equivalence (SYE) patches: SYEs refer to patches that are syntactically equivalent to the oracle
code but may differ in formatting or minor syntactic details. These patches do not alter the program’s behavior and
are considered valid fixes due to their structural similarity. For each PP and its corresponding oracle code snippets,
we removed comments and whitespace, then tokenized the resulting code snippets and replaced variable names with
generic placeholders. If the resulting sequences of tokens were identical, the patch was classified as an SYE.

3.2
Understand
Objective: The goal of the evaluation at the Understand layer is to assess whether SUEs can understand the underlying
bug logic by breaking down textually completely different code segments and identifying the known bug patterns
embedded within.
Approach: We leveraged LLMs to first analyze each bug instance from Defects4J and then to generate novel synthetic
bugs with corresponding test cases. These synthetic cases were created based on the LLM’s analysis of each bug (e.g.,
identifying similar error messages or the same root causes). This type of evaluation differs from the Apply layer, since
the datasets here are generated entirely by LLMs rather than injected into real-world projects. As a result, the bug
instances and their surrounding code context are textually distinct from both the original Defects4J programs and the
injected real-world variants, while still capturing the same failure logic. For our prototype, we picked a different LLM,
Claude 3.5 Sonnet, as our choice of LLMs to analyze the bugs and to generate synthetic datasets. We pick Claude 3.5
Sonnet due to its high quality and also to avoid potential bias and data contamination with our case study experiments
in Section 4. We have generated two groups of synthetic datasets:
• Synthetic Bugs with the same Root Causes: For each bug instance in Defects4J, we supplied Claude with the same
bug metadata, but prompted the model to identify the root causes. Then, based on the root causes of the bug, we
prompted Claude 3.5 Sonnet again to generate five sets of buggy code, bug fixes, and their corresponding test cases.
The Understand row in Figure 2 shows an example of a synthetically generated bug with the same root cause (a.k.a.,
a number format parsing failure) as the JacksonCore-5 issue.

Evaluation Schemes: To systematically evaluate the effectiveness of the SUEs, we have established the following clas-
sification of the SUE behavior while fixing a particular bug instance in Defects4J under different versions synthetically
created by Claude.
• 𝐹𝐼𝑋0 indicates that none of the injected bugs were fixed, suggesting the SUE cannot handle this bug type.
• 𝐹𝐼𝑋1 indicates that only one of the injected bugs was fixed, reflecting limited capability.
• 𝐹𝐼𝑋+ indicates that more than one, but not all, bugs were fixed, suggesting constrained capability.
• 𝐹𝐼𝑋𝐴indicates that all injected bugs were fixed, demonstrating high proficiency in handling this bug type.
This classification allows for a nuanced assessment of patch efficacy, facilitating a clearer understanding of SUE’s

3.3
Apply
Objective: The goal of the evaluation at the Apply layer is to determine whether the SUEs can understand the logic of
the code and subsequently apply the right bug-fixing patterns to bugs that they have previously seen but been perturbed
with lexical variations.
Approach: Various behavior-preserving code transformations can be applied here, so that the textual context of the
code is altered while keeping the runtime behavior the same. As shown in previous studies, LLM-powered SE solutions
can be brittle even in response to small code perturbations [66, 71, 83]. We only applied the simple code transformation
actions (variable and function renaming) here to check whether SUEs even possess the basic ability to understand the
logic behind the code. Altering variable names aims to check whether the SUEs understand the internal logical flow of
the code within a function, and altering function names aims to check whether the SUEs understand the function-level
dependencies. These two types of renaming schemes were applied:
(1) Rephrasing-based renaming: Depending on the context of the code, alternative function and variable names are
given. The rephrased variable/function names can be misleading or contextually different from the original
names. Hence, the SUEs must understand the bug in context and reconcile potentially tricky naming cues to fix
the bugs.
(2) Hash-based renaming: Instead of texts that can be read and parsed for meaning, renaming function/variable names
with cryptic hash values forces the SUEs to comprehend the underlying logic behind the code, as these names
are no longer meaningful and cannot provide any clues regarding the purpose or the concrete implementation of
the buggy code. This tests whether the SUEs understand the logic of the bug only through the structure and
semantics of the code.

3.4
Analyze
Objective: The goal of the evaluation at the Analyze layer is to check whether SUEs can analyze new project contexts
with different build systems while adopting learned fixing strategies, dependencies, and usage scenarios.
Approach: At the Apply layer, we kept the code context the same by performing the code transformation actions on
buggy code in the same project as the original benchmark. Here, we intended to evaluate the SUE’s performance by
checking whether it can recognize the buggy patterns and apply the corresponding fixes for bugs from completely
different project contexts. This is more challenging as, in addition to understanding the structure and the logic of the
corresponding code snippets, the SUEs also need to take the coding context (e.g., external dependencies, deployment
environment, and usage scenarios) into consideration. To ensure the freshness of our evaluation datasets, we intended
to inject new bugs, which have the same characteristics as our benchmark datasets, into real-world projects. Our steps
are listed below:

to explicitly filter them and output up to five candidate code snippets for each bug instance from the original
Defects4J benchmark. Since some bug instances do not have any matches with the real-world projects (e.g.,
Cli-5), and some have less than five matches (e.g., only two matches for the Cli-11 bug), we ended up with a
total of 261 code snippets from 37 real-world GitHub projects.
• Step 2 - Bug Injection: We used LLMs to inject bugs through few-shot prompting. For our research prototype, all
of the obtained code snippets from the previous step correspond to the fixed version of the selected bug instances.
We used GPT-4o to inject bugs into these code snippets by supplying the corresponding bugs and their bug fixes
from the Defects4J bug instances.
• Step 3 - Test Case Generation: Similar to the previous step, for each injected bug instance, we used LLMs to
generate the corresponding test cases through few-shot prompting. We then reused the existing test harness
from 36 out of the 37 selected real-world GitHub projects, inserting the newly generated test cases into them.
The one remaining project, BitStream [70], does not have any test cases. Therefore, we must develop its test
harness before injecting the newly generated tests.
• Step 4 - Verification and Refinement: The resulting buggy and bug-fixed versions were compiled and tested to
ensure the validity of the bug/bug-fixing pairs and the effectiveness of the generated test cases. Whenever
compilation errors or test execution issues arose (e.g., the test failing to reveal the bug or still failing on the fixed

fundamental limitation: current LLM-powered APR solutions remain brittle when confronted with diverse coding

controlled benchmarks.
5
Discussions and Result Implications
5.1
Assessment Summary
Our case study shows that while current LLM-powered APR solutions demonstrate some reasoning ability when
addressing synthetic bugs, they largely rely on memorized patterns to generate patches. SUEs often output the same
fixed code without considering the specific context. For instance, both 𝐶ℎ𝑎𝑡𝑅𝑒𝑝𝑎𝑖𝑟𝐺𝑃𝑇and 𝐶𝑖𝑔𝑎𝑅𝐺𝑃𝑇repeatedly
produced identical fixes for the Compress-7 bug, even when function names were renamed in the Apply layer. Although
both SUEs employ iterative refinement using sophisticated workflows and feedback, such as compilation and test
results, these mechanisms proved ineffective, as they continued to use the original function names. This highlights two
key limitations of current LLM-powered APR solutions: (1) insufficient understanding of code structure and syntax,
and (2) difficulty adapting to complex, real-world project contexts. Novel techniques are needed to enhance the code
comprehension and context awareness capabilities, either at the model or the agent level.
5.2
Patch Assessment in the Context of FM-powered APR Solutions
Since ChatRepair and CigaR only generate patches that pass the pre-existing test cases, they cannot accurately assess
the correctness of their own outputs. Moreover, our manual analysis at the Understand layer reveals that many PPs
generated by these APR solutions are in fact invalid. Unfortunately, none of the existing patch assessment and selection
works (e.g., [40, 41, 87]) have focused on patches generated from FM-based solutions, whose characteristics can differ
substantially from those of rule-based or deep-learning-based APR solutions. Further research is needed in this area in
order to ensure FM-powered APR solutions are safe for practical use.
5.3
Evaluating the Capabilities of APR Solutions beyond Defects4J, ChatRepair, and CigaR
Our research prototype was demonstrated on the Defects4J benchmark, but the framework applies to other APR
benchmarks as well. For instance, we executed SWE-agent [79], a popular LLM-powered agentic solution, a transformed
version of SWE-bench [34], which is a Python-based APR benchmark. Our experimental results also showed a significant

5.4
Benchmark Adaption Strategies
For each bug in the original benchmark, our framework generates multiple variations to support robust evaluation.
New strategies can be continuously added to better assess LLM-powered APR capabilities. For example, the current
Understand layer focuses on evaluating SUEs’ ability to comprehend code structure and syntax. In BloomAPR, only
renaming schemes have been applied to Defects4J so far. To enrich this layer, changes to code comments can also be
introduced. Our initial experiments show that adding or removing textual comments significantly impacts the SUE
performance. Similarly, code refactoring or injecting code smells can also be incorporated to alter or further complicate
the project context at the Apply and/or Analyze layers.
5.5
Using Bloom’s Taxonomy to Evaluate LLM-powered Software Engineering Solutions
In this paper, we emphasize the urgent need to update static benchmarks, which make up the majority of current SE
benchmarks, into dynamically evolving ones to more faithfully assess and improve the capabilities of LLM-powered
SE solutions. Instead of focusing solely on eliminating overlap with LLM training data, adapting static benchmarks
using Bloom’s Taxonomy offers a promising path for comprehensive evaluation. While our framework is demonstrated
on the APR benchmark Defects4J, it is also applicable to many other SE use cases, such as test case generation (e.g.,
TestGenEval [29]) and vulnerability detection (e.g., Vul4J [8], Big-Vul [19]).
6
Threats to Validity
Internal Validity: While evaluating the capabilities of LLM-powered APR solutions, we identified two primary sources
of potential confounding factors: (1) Data Contamination: we established an upper-bound baseline by evaluating SUEs
on the original Defects4J benchmark, which likely overlapped with the training datasets from the underlying LLMs
due to its long-standing public availability. We then evaluated SUEs on dynamically generated bugs that are textually
and contextually distinct but semantically similar to the original bugs. By comparing evaluation results across these bug
datasets, we measured the potential impact of data contamination. (2) Bug Characteristics: To ensure fair comparison
across different BloomAPR layers, all dynamically generated bugs were crafted to preserve key bug characteristics (e.g.,
root causes, bug fixing patterns, and triggering test failures). This consistency enables reliable cross-layer analysis and
interpretation of evaluation results.
External Validity: Choice of LLMs and Agents: This paper presents a framework for transforming static SE
benchmarks into dynamic benchmarks structured by Bloom’s Taxonomy. We demonstrated its effectiveness by evaluating
two state-of-the-art LLM-powered APR agents (ChatRepair and CigaR) using our prototype, BloomAPR, a Bloom’s
Taxonomy-based dynamic benchmark derived from the Java-based Defects4J dataset. There are many LLM-powered
APR agents (e.g., OpenHand [64], SWE-agent [79], and AutoCodeRover [85]) introduced recently. However, these
agents’ implementations are often tightly coupled with a specific benchmark (e.g., SWE-Bench) [38], causing difficulties
in cross-comparison with other APR agents causing difficulties in cross-comparison with other APR agents which are
designed for other benchmarks or evaluation criteria. To demonstrate the generalizability of our framework, we also
applied BloomAPR to another benchmark (SWE-Bench) using a different APR agent (SWE-agent) and observed similar

and cost over $14,000, despite extensive pipeline optimization and parallelization. We emphasize that our goal is not

Generalizability of Empirical Findings: Since our evaluation focuses specifically on Java-based function-level
bugs, the findings may not generalize to other programming languages (e.g., JavaScript or Haskell) or bug types (e.g.,
performance or security bugs). Additionally, results from this case study may not extend to non-LLM-powered APR
solutions (e.g., rule-based systems) or LLM-powered agents operating in other SE tasks (e.g., code review or requirements
analysis).
Construct Validity: Evaluation Metrics Our study adopts PP, SYE, and EM as the primary evaluation metrics,
consistent with prior works in this area [3, 7, 14, 31, 33, 43, 46, 69, 77, 80–82]. While these metrics help estimate patch
quality, they have limitations: passing test cases does not guarantee correctness, and multiple valid fixes may exist for
the same bug. Further research is needed to develop automated techniques capable of reliably assessing the correctness
of patches generated by LLM-powered APR solutions.
Identifier names: Variable and function names often carry semantic meaning. Prior studies [66, 71, 83] show
that meaning variable and/or function names aid LLMs in understanding code better. Our program perturbations
(rephrasing-based renaming and hash-based renaming) at the Understand layer intend to deliberately test whether
agents rely on superficial identifiers versus deep reasoning about the code logic.
Function name rephrasing is content-based, while variable name rephrasing is self-referential. These approaches
were designed to preserve semantic meaning. We manually verified that these changes did not alter the intended
meaning when developing our framework. The goal here is to evaluate whether APR agents can comprehend code
logic and apply correct bug-fixing patterns for familiar bugs.
Bug Injections: The bugs in the Apply and Analyze layers are injected into project contexts distinct from the
original Defects4J dataset. To objectively measure their capabilities, we selected up to five diverse project contexts
for each Defects4J bug (e.g., JacksonCore-5) and injected the same bug into each of them. Hence, there is always a
one-to-one correspondence between the original bugs in Defects4J to the injected bugs. We then assessed how many
contexts each APR agent could successfully fix (𝐹𝐼𝑋0/𝐹𝐼𝑋1/𝐹𝐼𝑋+/𝐹𝐼𝑋𝐴) as a proxy for their mastery of that specific
bug-fixing technique.
7
Conclusion
LLM-powered APR solutions have shown promising results in recent years, yet their evaluation still relies heavily on
static benchmarks such as Defects4J and SWE-bench. These benchmarks suffer from critical limitations, including the
risk of data contamination and a lack of contextual diversity needed to robustly assess reasoning capabilities. In this
paper, we propose BloomAPR, a novel dynamic evaluation framework grounded in Bloom’s Taxonomy, which enables
structured assessment across six levels of cognitive complexity. Applying BloomAPR to evaluate ChatRepair and CigaR
across multiple LLMs, we found that while these solutions perform well on synthetically generated bugs, they struggle
with realistic, context-rich scenarios. Their heavy reliance on memorized patterns results in substantial performance
drops under minor code perturbations and project context shifts.
Our study highlights key limitations of current LLM-powered APR solutions and the benchmarks used to assess
them. It calls for broader adoption of dynamic, Bloom-based evaluation methods to better understand and enhance the
robustness, generalizability, and reasoning capabilities of AI-driven software engineering tools.

key_findings.claim: LLM-powered APR solutions heavily rely on memorized patterns from training data, with Defects4J confirmed in the training data of all three evaluated LLMs (GPT-3.5-turbo, Llama-3.1, StarCoder2).
key_findings.quantitative_result: 53.92% to 81.57% plausible patch rate at the Remember layer across 6 APR configurations
key_findings.context: Remember layer evaluation on 217 Defects4J v2.1.0 bug instances; prompt extraction attack confirmed memorization in GPT and Llama

key_findings.claim: APR solutions show a counterintuitive performance increase on synthetically generated bugs that preserve root causes but use novel code, indicating inflated benchmark scores driven by memorization rather than genuine comprehension.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Up to 60.66% increase in PP at the Understand layer compared to Remember layer
key_findings.context: Synthetic bugs generated by Claude 3.5 Sonnet; FIX+ + FIXA combined to represent consistent fixing ability

key_findings.claim: Many plausible patches generated at the Understand layer are actually invalid upon manual inspection, passing existing test cases but failing to capture true program semantics.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Significant drop in SYE (20.60% to 83.78% decrease) and EM (11.53% to 80.96% decrease) from Remember to Understand layer
key_findings.context: Manual sampling of PP instances; example: ChatRepairGPT fixing all Cli-2 variants with semantically incorrect patches

key_findings.claim: Behavior-preserving variable and function renaming (Apply layer) causes substantial performance degradation in APR solutions, indicating they parse code as natural language rather than reasoning over program structure.
key_findings.quantitative_result: 37.86% to 63.76% drop in PP vs Remember layer; hash-based renaming causes 54.11%/64.95%/65.94% average drop in PP/SYE/EM, rephrasing-based 43.77%/44.09%/49.72%
key_findings.context: Six benchmark variants generated via Eclipse AST renaming; McNemar's test confirms statistical significance (p<0.05) for all differences

key_findings.claim: Injecting bugs into real-world project contexts (Analyze layer) causes the most severe performance degradation, revealing fundamental generalization limitations of LLM-powered APR solutions.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Average 56.59% drop in PP vs Remember layer; 40.38% to 74.04% of bugs result in FIX0 (no variants fixed); only 13.46% to 41.34% PP rate
key_findings.context: 261 code snippets from 37 real-world GitHub projects; bugs injected via GPT-4o few-shot prompting with verification loop

key_findings.claim: Function renaming affects PP and SYE more strongly than variable renaming, while variable renaming disproportionately impacts Exact Match rates.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Function renaming: 34.23%/26.72% average drop in PP/SYE; variable renaming: 26.32%/23.05% drop in PP/SYE but 62.50% drop in EM vs 27.02% for function renaming
key_findings.context: Ablation study at the Apply layer separating function-only vs variable-only renaming effects

key_findings.claim: CigaR's multi-stage self-reflection architecture outperforms ChatRepair's two-stage reflection in generating valid patches at the Understand layer.
key_findings.quantitative_result: CigaR shows 2.39%-10.64% higher PP, 74.07%-366.67% higher SYE, and 83.33%-475.00% higher EM vs ChatRepair using same LLM
key_findings.context: Understand layer comparison across all three LLMs; highlights agent architecture independent of underlying LLM

key_findings.claim: Agentic workflows (reflection, test-time sampling, iterative debugging) do not automatically mitigate data contamination effects in LLM-powered APR solutions.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Both ChatRepairGPT and CigaRGPT repeatedly produced identical fixes for Compress-7 even when function names were renamed at the Apply layer
key_findings.context: First systematic evaluation of agentic mechanisms under contamination in a controlled setting

key_findings.claim: BloomAPR generalizes beyond CigaR and ChatRepair: SWE-agent on a transformed SWE-bench shows up to 92.61% performance drop between Remember and Understand layers.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Up to 92.61% performance drop between Remember and Understand layers for SWE-agent on SWE-bench
key_findings.context: Preliminary validation on Python-based SWE-bench; demonstrates framework generalizability across languages and benchmarks

key_findings.claim: The compound effect of logical and lexical variations on APR performance is far greater than either variation type alone.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Applying hash-based renaming to synthetic bugs caused majority to become unfixable, while simple renaming alone or synthetic bugs alone were partially fixable
key_findings.context: Controlled experiment applying renaming to Understand-layer synthetic bugs to isolate interaction effects

llm_extraction.methods_summary: BloomAPR is a dynamic evaluation framework that transforms static APR benchmarks into structured assessments aligned with Bloom's Taxonomy's six cognitive layers (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create). The prototype implements four layers using Defects4J v2.1.0 as base (217 single-function Java bugs). Remember: original benchmark bugs with membership inference. Understand: LLM-generated synthetic bugs with same root causes (5 variants per bug) using Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Apply: behavior-preserving AST-based renaming (rephrasing via GPT-4o, hash-based via SHA-256) creating 6 benchmark variants. Analyze: bug injection into 261 code snippets from 37 real-world GitHub projects via GPT-4o few-shot prompting with compile/test verification loop. Two SOTA APR solutions evaluated: ChatRepair and CigaR, each under three LLMs (GPT-3.5-turbo-1106, Llama-3.1-70B, StarCoder2-15B-Instruct-v0.1). Metrics: % bugs with Plausible Patches (PP), SYntactic Equivalence (SYE), and Exact Match (EM). McNemar's test used for statistical significance testing across layers. Total experimental cost exceeded $14,000 over three months.
llm_extraction.limitations: Only four of six Bloom's Taxonomy layers implemented; Evaluate and Create layers not addressed. Evaluation confined to Java function-level bugs from Defects4J, limiting generalizability to other languages (JavaScript, Haskell), bug types (performance, security), and file/repo-level repair. Only two APR agents (ChatRepair, CigaR) studied in depth, though SWE-agent was partially validated. PP, SYE, and EM metrics do not guarantee patch correctness since tests may be incomplete. Synthetic bug generation relies on LLMs (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o), introducing potential quality variance despite manual verification. Copilot code search occasionally hallucinated projects, requiring explicit filtering; some Defects4J bugs had no real-world matches. Results from the Analyze layer may be confounded by GPT-4o bias in both bug injection and test generation. The evaluation cost and scale may limit replication by other groups.

relationships.description: BloomAPR evaluates ChatRepair across four cognitive layers, revealing its reliance on memorization and brittleness under code perturbations beyond the original Defects4J benchmark setting
BloomAPR transforms the static Defects4J benchmark into a dynamic, multi-layer evaluation environment by generating synthetic variants, renaming schemes, and real-world bug injections
BloomAPR confirms and extends findings that LLMs memorize bug benchmarks, additionally showing this memorization is embedded in agentic APR workflows not just direct prompting
BloomAPR corroborates that LLM-powered SE solutions are brittle to code perturbations, extending this finding from code generation to APR agents with agentic workflows
BloomAPR adapts the dynamic benchmarking philosophy of DyVal (DAG-based reasoning) to the APR domain using Bloom's Taxonomy as the structuring framework
BloomAPR demonstrates its framework generalizes to SWE-bench by applying it to SWE-agent, showing similar performance degradation patterns across Remember and Understand layers
BloomAPR addresses RepairBench's static limitation by dynamically generating benchmark variants that maintain semantic consistency while providing fresh evaluation scenarios

methodology_details.approach: Dynamic benchmark construction using Bloom's Taxonomy to transform static APR benchmark (Defects4J v2.1.0) into four evaluation layers: (1) original bugs as baseline, (2) LLM-synthesized semantic variants, (3) AST-based lexical perturbation via two renaming schemes, (4) bug injection into real-world project contexts with automated verification
datasets: BloomAPR Understand layer: ~1085 synthetic bug variants generated by Claude 3.5 Sonnet
BloomAPR Apply layer: 6 benchmark variants via AST renaming (rephrasing + hash-based × variable/function/both)
BloomAPR Analyze layer: 261 code snippets from 37 real-world GitHub projects
metrics: FIX0/FIX1/FIX+/FIXA classification for Understand and Analyze layers
McNemar's test p-value for cross-layer comparisons
methodology_details.reproducibility_notes: Replication package shared at [1] (URL not disclosed in paper). Experiments cost over $14,000 and took three months. Membership inference via StarCoder dataset utility and prompt extraction attack. Eclipse AST package used for renaming; GPT-4o for rephrasing names; SHA-256 with timestamp for hash names. Manual verification of synthetic bugs and injected bug/fix pairs.
